message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing images, now also for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few (2–32) high‑performance cores. | Hundreds to thousands of smaller, simpler cores. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or lightly parallel; each core can handle complex branching and large caches. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – many cores execute the same instruction on different data simultaneously. |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (≈2–4 GHz) because each core does more work per cycle. | Lower clock speeds (≈0.5–1 GHz) because each core is simpler. |
| **Cache & memory** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, fast access to main memory. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, supports branching, exceptions, and a wide range of operations. | Simpler, optimized for arithmetic and data‑parallel operations. |
| **Typical workloads** | Operating system, database queries, web servers, general software. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for single‑thread performance; less efficient when many threads run concurrently. | Highly efficient for data‑parallel tasks; can process many operations per watt. |

In short, a CPU is a versatile “master” processor that excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks, while a GPU is a specialized “worker” that shines when you need to perform the same operation on a huge number of data elements at once. This specialization makes GPUs indispensable for modern graphics, AI, and high‑performance computing workloads.
